activities.caption: one loud stranger — land the dragged mean on the track
activities.name: ddNoticePlace

config.prompt: The set {2, 4, 6, 8, x} with x dragged up to 1,000: place the marker where the mean now sits.
config.why: The mean is dragged a fifth of the way toward the extreme: (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 1000) ÷ 5 = 204 — while the median never leaves 6. That asymmetry is the argument for median income.

activities.caption: one claim about the chase is wrong — click it
activities.name: ddMiniSpot

config.prompt: One line of this outlier anatomy is wrong — click it:
lines: The set {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} has mean 6 and median 6 — perfect agreement.
Drag the fifth value to 1,000: the mean becomes (2 + 4 + 6 + 8 + 1,000) ÷ 5 = 204.
The median rises with it, to about 204 as well.
An extreme value moves the mean by its excess over the others, divided by the count.
The median only moves if the extreme value crosses the middle.
config.correction: The median stays frozen at 6 — nothing crossed the middle; only the mean chases the outlier, dragging four calm values up with it.
config.why: Rank is the median's whole diet: no crossing, no movement — which is why news reports that quietly swap mean for median are editing the story.

activities.caption: call the grouped mean before the midpoints do
activities.name: ddGroupEst

config.prompt: Waiting times arrive pre-bucketed: 0–10 min (14 customers), 10–20 (22), 20–30 (12), 30–40 (2). Call the estimated mean, in minutes.
config.context: The modal class 10–20 already hints the mean sits in the teens — the estimate is honest only if values really cluster near midpoints.

activities.caption: a table of shoe sizes — rebuild the three answers in order
activities.name: ddFreqOrder

config.prompt: Ungrouped frequency table: sizes 6, 7, 8, 9 with frequencies 3, 9, 7, 1 — order the computations:
items: Mode: the value with the highest frequency — 7, appearing 9 times
Median position: (n + 1) ÷ 2 = 20 + 1 over 2 = the 10.5th ordered item
Median: between the 9th item (a 7) and the 10th (an 8), so median = 7
config.why: Mode by counting, mean by weighting, median by position — one table, three different questions.

config.text: Grouped median by interpolation: median = L + ((n/2 − %%0%%) ÷ %%1%%) × %%2%% — here 10 + ((25 − 14) ÷ 22) × 10 ≈ 15.0 minutes.
config.hint: L is the class's lower boundary; the other three symbols are defined in the sentence just before the formula.

activities.caption: true or false — the price of buckets
activities.name: ddMidJudge

statements.s: Grouped-data formulas produce estimates, and an exam answer should say so.
statements.why: Bucketed data has lost the raw values; midpoint and interpolation are the best recovery of it, not a recovery of all of it.

statements.s: A bucket whose members bunch near its lower boundary makes the midpoint mean estimate too high.
statements.why: The estimate is honest only if values really cluster near midpoints — bunching at an edge biases it.

statements.s: Grouping recovers all of the information the raw data contained.
statements.why: It always costs information; the formulas are the best recovery, not a complete one.

activities.anchor: exam marks live in the justification
activities.caption: pair the dataset with its honest summary
activities.name: ddPairSort

config.prompt: Which centre-and-spread pairing does each dataset deserve?

items.label: clean, roughly symmetric data with no extreme values
incomes — a few enormous fortunes stretch the tail
the shirt size the shop must stock
commute times with two peaks, from two different towns
house prices — a few mansions among many flats
bell-shaped exam marks feeding the 68–95–99.7 rule

config.why: Two diagnostics settle it: compare the mean to the median (a big gap signals skew or outliers) and look at the tail's direction.

activities.caption: you are the reader — walk the two traps
activities.name: ddMisleadBranch

config.root: Two summaries of the same institution land on your desk. Walk the defence.

start.text: A bar chart makes a 1% difference look like a landslide. First move?

choices.label: Check where the y-axis starts
choices.feedback: A bar chart starting at 90 instead of 0 is the classic landslide-maker.

choices.label: Check how the groups were aggregated
choices.feedback: Aggregation is the other place summaries go quiet.

choices.label: Bars are decorative — read the numbers
choices.feedback: The picture is the claim here: the truncation manufactures the gap.

agg.text: The overall number reverses inside every subgroup.

choices.label: Trust the disaggregated story — this is Simpson's paradox
choices.feedback: Berkeley 1973: women applied disproportionately to the most competitive programmes, and the disaggregated answer was the truth.

choices.label: Average the subgroups back together
choices.feedback: That reproduces the reversal — the aggregate is the artifact.

fixed.text: Defused. One question covers both traps: what did the summary discard to look that way?

duped.text: Duped — a truncated axis manufactures a landslide, and a bad aggregation manufactures a reversal. Ask what was discarded.

config.why: The aggregate answer and the disaggregated answer can be opposite — and only one of them is the truth.
